title: What a service package's compose fragment may declare — contract v1
description: An allowlist, checked twice: by tools/compose-check.mjs in stackvo-service-packages before a package is published, and by compose_policy.rs in the app after a fragment is rendered and before it is assembled. Both read THIS file so the two cannot drift. See docs/servis-market-mimarisi.md §4.4.
why: Until service packages existed, StackVo only ever handed Docker files that were compiled into its own binary. A package is data somebody else wrote, and a compose service is not a passive description — the right four words in it are root on the host.
An allowlist rather than a blocklist, because the list of things worth forbidding is only ever known in retrospect. A key nobody has considered is refused, and adding it is a review.
Checked AFTER rendering, not before. What a template puts inside {{ settings.X }} is only visible once X has a value, and X is a field a user can type into.

allowed.image: The image to run. Its registry is checked separately against policy.market.allowedRegistries.
allowed.container_name: Derived per instance by the app; a fragment writes {{ instance.container }} and nothing else.
allowed.environment: Environment variables. Values come from the manifest's settings, which is the whole render context a fragment gets.
allowed.ports: Published ports. The host half is allocated by the app, so a fragment writes {{ port.<name> }}.
allowed.expose: Ports visible only on the Docker network.
allowed.volumes: Named volumes and generated config files only — see rules.volumes below.
allowed.networks: The workspace network and the instance's aliases.
allowed.depends_on: Ordering against a companion or another instance.
allowed.labels: Traefik routing. Router and service names are per instance.
allowed.user: The uid the process runs as.
allowed.cap_add: Linux capabilities, from a short list; see rules.cap_add. Listed here rather than under `refused` because a key that carries a rule is a key that may appear — the rule is what narrows it. Written the other way round first, and the effect was that the exception the rule described could never be reached: SYS_ADMIN and several others are root by another name; see rules.cap_add for the exception.
allowed.stop_grace_period: How long a stop waits before it kills.
allowed.shm_size: Shared memory size — Postgres and Chrome-based images need it raised.
allowed.deploy: Resource reservations and limits only; see rules.deploy.
allowed.sysctls: Kernel parameters, from a narrow list; see rules.sysctls.
allowed.init: Run an init process as PID 1.
allowed.read_only: A read-only root filesystem, which is a hardening measure and never a risk.

refused.network_mode: `host` removes network isolation entirely, and no other value is worth the exception.
refused.pid: `host` puts the container in the host's process namespace.
refused.cgroup_parent: Places the container in a cgroup the app does not own.
refused.devices: Direct access to a host device.
refused.security_opt: `apparmor:unconfined` and `seccomp:unconfined` switch off the kernel's own defences.
refused.build: A local build context is arbitrary compilation and arbitrary downloading, decided by the package.
refused.extends: Reaches into a file this validator has not seen.
refused.env_file: Reads a file this validator has not seen, into an environment it has approved.
refused.volumes_from: Inherits another container's mounts, including ones this policy refused.
refused.platform: Silently pulls an image for another architecture.
refused.external_links: Links to containers outside this stack.
refused.healthcheck: Written by the app from the manifest's `health` block, the way `image` and `profiles` are — so a fragment declaring one is a second author for the field `depends_on: condition: service_healthy` reads. Two of them in one service is a duplicate YAML key; one of them wins and nothing says which. The manifest form is also constrained where the fragment form is not: the schema requires a list, and Compose runs the string form through a shell.

volumes.namedVolume: A volume handle the manifest declares, written {{ volume.<name> }}. The app derives the real name per instance.
volumes.generatedFile: A config file the manifest declares, written {{ file.<name> }}. The app renders it under <root>/generated/configs/<instance>/ and mounts it read-only.
volumes.instanceLogs: {{ instance.logs }} — the instance's own log directory under <root>/logs/services/.
volumes.refused: Anything else. A literal host path is a bind mount the package chose, and `/var/run/docker.sock` is root on the host with an extra step.

cap_add.why: IPC_LOCK is Elasticsearch's memlock and the rest are what an image needs to drop privileges to its own user. SYS_ADMIN, SYS_PTRACE, NET_ADMIN and NET_RAW are deliberately not here.

sysctls.why: vm.max_map_count is Elasticsearch's, and it is the one everybody hits. The others are ordinary tuning. Anything else is a kernel parameter a package should not be choosing on somebody's laptop.

deploy.why: Limits and reservations are useful and harmless. `placement`, `mode` and `replicas` are Swarm, which this app does not run, and a fragment that sets them is a fragment written for somewhere else.

labels.why: The only labels a package has any business writing are routing ones. A label is metadata other tooling reads, and a package should not be able to tag a container as something it is not.

image.why: The reference is assembled by the app from the manifest's registry, repository, tag and digest — which is where the registry allowlist and the digest pin are applied. A fragment writing a literal image would bypass both.
